title: Ecosystem Disturbance and Recovery Core Test
description: Use before-and-after data, food webs, and comparison sites to explain ecosystem responses to disturbance and evaluate recovery.

questions.prompt: A storm removes many trees from a woodland. Which is a direct physical change?
questions.questionText: A storm removes many trees from a woodland. Which is a direct physical change?
options: Every herbivore population immediately doubles.
More sunlight reaches the ground where canopy was lost.
The soil must lose all living organisms.
All species experience the same change in food.
questions.correctAnswer: More sunlight reaches the ground where canopy was lost.
questions.explanation: Canopy loss directly changes ground-level light; population responses depend on other factors.

questions.prompt: A fire removes vegetation but leaves much soil and some roots. Which condition can help plants return?
questions.questionText: A fire removes vegetation but leaves much soil and some roots. Which condition can help plants return?
options: All recovery must begin on bare rock.
Plants no longer need water after disturbance.
The former species must all return at the same time.
Surviving roots and soil can support regrowth.
questions.correctAnswer: Surviving roots and soil can support regrowth.
questions.explanation: What remains after a disturbance influences recovery; surviving roots can matter.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines ecological succession?
questions.questionText: Which description best defines ecological succession?
options: An individual growing taller during one afternoon.
Changes in a community's composition over time as conditions and interactions change.
A community always returning to an identical final state.
All organisms moving away at the same instant.
questions.correctAnswer: Changes in a community's composition over time as conditions and interactions change.
questions.explanation: Succession concerns community change, not a guaranteed fixed endpoint.

questions.prompt: A food web shows grass -> insects -> small birds, with arrows for food transfer. A disturbance reduces grass. Which effect could follow?
questions.questionText: A food web shows grass -> insects -> small birds, with arrows for food transfer. A disturbance reduces grass. Which effect could follow?
options: Reduced food for insects may later reduce food for birds.
Birds necessarily increase because there is less grass.
Insects receive more energy from the smaller grass supply.
The bird response must happen before the grass change.
questions.correctAnswer: Reduced food for insects may later reduce food for birds.
questions.explanation: Connected food supplies can create delayed indirect effects.

questions.prompt: What is a useful baseline for studying a flood's effects?
questions.questionText: What is a useful baseline for studying a flood's effects?
options: Only the highest population count after the flood.
Only a photograph of a different habitat after the flood.
Measurements of the same habitat before the flood.
A prediction written after all results were known.
questions.correctAnswer: Measurements of the same habitat before the flood.
questions.explanation: A baseline provides a pre-disturbance comparison.

questions.prompt: A plot is green again, but one grass species now dominates where many plants grew. What can be concluded?
questions.questionText: A plot is green again, but one grass species now dominates where many plants grew. What can be concluded?
options: Every aspect of the ecosystem has recovered.
All original species must be present under the grass.
Green cover proves food webs are unchanged.
Plant cover returned, but species composition may not have recovered.
questions.correctAnswer: Plant cover returned, but species composition may not have recovered.
questions.explanation: Cover and community composition are different measures of recovery.

questions.prompt: Before a flood, a site had 40 shrubs. One month later it had 10; six months later it had 22. Which statement is supported?
questions.questionText: Before a flood, a site had 40 shrubs. One month later it had 10; six months later it had 22. Which statement is supported?
options: Shrub count fully recovered within six months.
Shrub count partly recovered but remained below the baseline.
Shrub count continued falling throughout the study.
The flood caused no change because shrubs remained.
questions.correctAnswer: Shrub count partly recovered but remained below the baseline.
questions.explanation: The count rose from 10 to 22 but was still below 40.

questions.prompt: Two plots lose vegetation. Plot A retains soil; Plot B is newly exposed bare rock. Why might A recover cover sooner?
questions.questionText: Two plots lose vegetation. Plot A retains soil; Plot B is newly exposed bare rock. Why might A recover cover sooner?
options: Its plants no longer need sunlight.
Bare rock always contains more roots.
Soil guarantees the same community within one week.
Its existing soil can provide water storage, nutrients, and surviving plant material.
questions.correctAnswer: Its existing soil can provide water storage, nutrients, and surviving plant material.
questions.explanation: Remaining resources and organisms can support faster establishment, without guaranteeing a timetable.

questions.prompt: A trail closes to reduce trampling. What comparison best tests its effect on vegetation?
questions.questionText: A trail closes to reduce trampling. What comparison best tests its effect on vegetation?
options: Compare one closed wet site to one open dry site only afterward.
Count visitors but never measure vegetation.
Track similar closed and open trail edges before and after closure.
Measure only the closed site's tallest plant once.
questions.correctAnswer: Track similar closed and open trail edges before and after closure.
questions.explanation: Matched sites and baseline measurements help distinguish closure effects from wider changes.

questions.prompt: A diagram shows canopy loss -> more ground light -> more sun-loving seedlings. What must be added to predict seedling success more carefully?
questions.questionText: A diagram shows canopy loss -> more ground light -> more sun-loving seedlings. What must be added to predict seedling success more carefully?
options: A rule that more light benefits every species equally.
A guarantee that all mature trees return immediately.
Water, soil conditions, and access to seeds or surviving plants.
An assumption that light supplies all plant matter.
questions.correctAnswer: Water, soil conditions, and access to seeds or surviving plants.
questions.explanation: Light is one factor; other resources and available organisms constrain the response.

questions.prompt: What makes frequent mowing different from one mowing followed by a long pause?
questions.questionText: What makes frequent mowing different from one mowing followed by a long pause?
options: Repeated removal can prevent plants from reaching later growth stages.
Repeated mowing has no effect once the first cut is over.
One cut always removes all soil permanently.
Both schedules must produce identical communities.
questions.correctAnswer: Repeated removal can prevent plants from reaching later growth stages.
questions.explanation: Disturbance frequency can change which plants persist or establish.

questions.prompt: A site gains plant species from 3 to 8 after a storm. Does this alone prove the storm improved every ecosystem function?
questions.questionText: A site gains plant species from 3 to 8 after a storm. Does this alone prove the storm improved every ecosystem function?
options: Yes; more species guarantees improvement in every function.
No; species number cannot ever be useful evidence.
No; species number is one measure and other functions were not measured.
Yes; the original species must all be among the eight.
questions.correctAnswer: No; species number is one measure and other functions were not measured.
questions.explanation: Richness is informative but does not establish the state of every function or species.

questions.prompt: Which factor helps explain different recovery at two burned sites?
questions.questionText: Which factor helps explain different recovery at two burned sites?
options: Both sites are called woodlands.
Both were photographed at noon.
Both maps use the same color.
One retains roots and nearby seed sources while the other lacks them.
questions.correctAnswer: One retains roots and nearby seed sources while the other lacks them.
questions.explanation: Surviving organisms and nearby sources can influence what returns.

questions.prompt: An untreated reference site falls from 100 to 80 insects while a disturbed site falls from 100 to 30. What does the reference reveal?
questions.questionText: An untreated reference site falls from 100 to 80 insects while a disturbed site falls from 100 to 30. What does the reference reveal?
options: All 70 lost insects at the disturbed site must be due to the disturbance.
Some decline may reflect shared conditions, while the disturbed site declined more.
The disturbance caused the reference site to lose exactly 20 insects.
The disturbed site lost fewer insects than the reference.
questions.correctAnswer: Some decline may reflect shared conditions, while the disturbed site declined more.
questions.explanation: A shared decline suggests wider factors may contribute; the excess decline needs interpretation.

questions.prompt: A woodland becomes shrubland after repeated droughts. Which idea does this challenge?
questions.questionText: A woodland becomes shrubland after repeated droughts. Which idea does this challenge?
options: Changing water availability can affect populations.
Communities can change over time.
Recovery always recreates the exact earlier community.
Repeated disturbances can influence recovery.
questions.correctAnswer: Recovery always recreates the exact earlier community.
questions.explanation: A changed environment can support a different community; return is not guaranteed.

questions.prompt: A site has 90% plant cover before disturbance, 20% immediately after, and 65% a year later. What additional evidence is most useful for judging habitat recovery?
questions.questionText: A site has 90% plant cover before disturbance, 20% immediately after, and 65% a year later. What additional evidence is most useful for judging habitat recovery?
options: Plant species identities and use of the site by other organisms.
Only a second estimate of the same final cover.
The site's distance from the photographer.
The number of words in the restoration plan.
questions.correctAnswer: Plant species identities and use of the site by other organisms.
questions.explanation: Composition and habitat use add dimensions that total cover misses.

questions.prompt: Which chain plausibly explains a delayed decline in insect-eating birds after vegetation removal?
questions.questionText: Which chain plausibly explains a delayed decline in insect-eating birds after vegetation removal?
options: Fewer host plants -> fewer insects -> less bird food.
Fewer host plants -> more insect food -> fewer birds.
Fewer birds -> earlier vegetation removal necessarily caused by birds.
More bare ground -> all birds lose feathers immediately.
questions.correctAnswer: Fewer host plants -> fewer insects -> less bird food.
questions.explanation: An indirect food-web pathway can create a lag between the disturbance and bird response.

questions.prompt: A restoration plot gains 12 species, but an untreated nearby plot gains 11 during a rainy year. What is the fairest conclusion?
questions.questionText: A restoration plot gains 12 species, but an untreated nearby plot gains 11 during a rainy year. What is the fairest conclusion?
options: The treatment caused all 12 species to arrive.
Rain cannot influence recovery in either plot.
Both improved; these counts alone show little evidence of a large additional treatment effect.
The treatment definitely failed because both plots improved.
questions.correctAnswer: Both improved; these counts alone show little evidence of a large additional treatment effect.
questions.explanation: The comparison suggests a large shared change, so treatment attribution should be limited.

questions.prompt: Two samples have equal total plant counts. One has five species; the other has one. Which recovery measure distinguishes them?
questions.questionText: Two samples have equal total plant counts. One has five species; the other has one. Which recovery measure distinguishes them?
options: Total individual count alone.
Species richness.
Number of sampling days alone.
Total plot area alone.
questions.correctAnswer: Species richness.
questions.explanation: Equal abundance can conceal different variety.

questions.prompt: A student sees more seedlings after a storm and claims more light caused them. Which competing explanation should be checked?
questions.questionText: A student sees more seedlings after a storm and claims more light caused them. Which competing explanation should be checked?
options: Seedlings were counted in the same units.
The data were recorded in a notebook.
The storm also delivered seeds and changed moisture.
The student used a ruler to mark the plot.
questions.correctAnswer: The storm also delivered seeds and changed moisture.
questions.explanation: Several changes occurred together, so the light mechanism is not isolated.

questions.prompt: Site A: 100 plants before, 20 after, 80 after a year. Site B: 100 before, 70 after, 75 after a year. Which comparison is correct?
questions.questionText: Site A: 100 plants before, 20 after, 80 after a year. Site B: 100 before, 70 after, 75 after a year. Which comparison is correct?
options: B retained more plants initially; A gained more plants during the following year.
A retained more plants initially; B gained more afterward.
Both resisted the initial disturbance equally.
B returned fully to its baseline.
questions.correctAnswer: B retained more plants initially; A gained more plants during the following year.
questions.explanation: Initial losses differ: A lost 80, B lost 30. Later gains are 60 and 5.

questions.prompt: A recovery model assumes that seeds are available nearby. A new road isolates the plot. Which prediction should be reconsidered?
questions.questionText: A recovery model assumes that seeds are available nearby. A new road isolates the plot. Which prediction should be reconsidered?
options: Whether plants still need water.
How readily plants can arrive from surrounding habitat.
Whether matter has mass.
Whether the original count was measured before the storm.
questions.correctAnswer: How readily plants can arrive from surrounding habitat.
questions.explanation: Isolation changes a model assumption about arrival, not basic plant requirements.

questions.prompt: After clearing, plant cover rises quickly but soil washes away during rain. Which conclusion fits both observations?
questions.questionText: After clearing, plant cover rises quickly but soil washes away during rain. Which conclusion fits both observations?
options: Vegetation cover is improving while soil stability remains a problem.
Fast cover increase proves soil recovery is complete.
Erosion proves no plant cover has returned.
Plant cover and soil loss must always move together.
questions.correctAnswer: Vegetation cover is improving while soil stability remains a problem.
questions.explanation: Different functions can recover at different rates; multiple indicators are needed.

questions.prompt: A proposal replants trees immediately after erosion removes topsoil. What evidence should inform the plan first?
questions.questionText: A proposal replants trees immediately after erosion removes topsoil. What evidence should inform the plan first?
options: Whether remaining soil and water conditions can support the chosen trees.
Whether the original trees had attractive names.
Whether planting is faster than monitoring.
Whether the plan contains the most seedlings regardless of survival.
questions.correctAnswer: Whether remaining soil and water conditions can support the chosen trees.
questions.explanation: Restoration must address conditions that limit establishment, not just add organisms.

questions.prompt: An invasive plant covers a restored plot. Total cover rises, but native host plants decline. What outcome is possible for insects that depend on those hosts?
questions.questionText: An invasive plant covers a restored plot. Total cover rises, but native host plants decline. What outcome is possible for insects that depend on those hosts?
options: Their food supply must rise with total cover.
All insects must disappear at once.
Host identity cannot affect their food supply.
Their food supply may decline despite the greater total cover.
questions.correctAnswer: Their food supply may decline despite the greater total cover.
questions.explanation: Species identity and feeding relationships matter; total vegetation alone is insufficient.

questions.prompt: A three-year recovery curve rises, then falls in year three. What is the best next step before declaring the original treatment harmful?
questions.questionText: A three-year recovery curve rises, then falls in year three. What is the best next step before declaring the original treatment harmful?
options: Discard year three because recovery should be smooth.
Check for new disturbances, changed weather, and matching reference-site trends.
Assume the original treatment is the only possible cause.
Use only the highest point as the final outcome.
questions.correctAnswer: Check for new disturbances, changed weather, and matching reference-site trends.
questions.explanation: Nonlinear recovery can reflect new conditions; causal claims need the relevant evidence.

questions.prompt: A study samples one 1-square-meter patch before restoration and ten such patches afterward, then compares totals. What is wrong?
questions.questionText: A study samples one 1-square-meter patch before restoration and ten such patches afterward, then compares totals. What is wrong?
options: Larger samples necessarily reduce all counts.
Plant density cannot be measured with plots.
Using more patches proves restoration caused growth.
Unequal sampled area can create an apparent increase without higher density.
questions.correctAnswer: Unequal sampled area can create an apparent increase without higher density.
questions.explanation: Comparable area or density is needed; totals across unequal effort are misleading.

questions.prompt: A model predicts shrubs then trees after clearing. Trees never establish during recurring dry years. How should the model change?
questions.questionText: A model predicts shrubs then trees after clearing. Trees never establish during recurring dry years. How should the model change?
options: Include water availability as a condition affecting the predicted sequence.
Keep the prediction because models cannot be revised.
State that shrubs turn into trees when conditions improve.
Remove every species interaction because one prediction failed.
questions.correctAnswer: Include water availability as a condition affecting the predicted sequence.
questions.explanation: Succession depends on conditions; plants do not transform into other species.

questions.prompt: Which evidence most strongly supports a closure helping plant recovery?
questions.questionText: Which evidence most strongly supports a closure helping plant recovery?
options: One closed site has one tall plant after a rainy week.
A closed site is greener than an open site measured in a different season.
Visitors say the closure looks helpful.
Replicated closed sites improve more than matched open sites from similar baselines across the same period.
questions.correctAnswer: Replicated closed sites improve more than matched open sites from similar baselines across the same period.
questions.explanation: Matched, repeated before-and-after comparisons better address alternatives and sampling variation.

questions.prompt: A recovery report shows cover back at baseline, half the former species, and continuing erosion. Which recommendation best fits?
questions.questionText: A recovery report shows cover back at baseline, half the former species, and continuing erosion. Which recommendation best fits?
options: Declare every ecosystem function fully restored.
Report cover recovery and continue addressing composition and soil stability.
Ignore cover because no part recovered.
Stop monitoring because one indicator reached its target.
questions.correctAnswer: Report cover recovery and continue addressing composition and soil stability.
questions.explanation: Recovery has multiple dimensions; partial success and remaining limitations can both be reported.
